records.name: ROC-AUC, PR-AUC and time-dependent AUC
records.tldr: ROC-AUC measures how a score orders cases and non-cases across thresholds. Ranking, calibrated probabilities and useful treatment decisions are separate questions.
records.summary: A receiver operating characteristic curve plots sensitivity against one minus specificity across thresholds for a defined binary condition. Its area measures case versus non-case ranking; with the stated convention, tied scores receive half credit. An area of 0.5 represents chance ordering and 1 perfect ordering in those data. AUC is not the proportion of individual predictions that are correct, and it does not establish calibrated probabilities or a useful decision threshold.

links.label: Wikipedia: precision and recall
Wikipedia
The meaning and use of the area under a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve.
Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve in Diagnostic Test Assessment
On the C-statistics for evaluating overall adequacy of risk prediction procedures with censored survival data.
Evaluation of clinical prediction models (part 2): how to undertake an external validation study.
FDA: statistical guidance for reporting diagnostic-test studies

notes: Fictional case scores are 0.9 and 0.6; non-case scores are 0.7 and 0.2. Three of four case/non-case pairs have the higher case score, giving AUC 0.75, also the area under the stepped ROC curve. Squaring these positive scores preserves their ordering and AUC while changing their numerical probability values. The example therefore separates ranking from calibration. Half-credit for tied scores is an explicit convention; an observed AUC is an estimate with uncertainty, not a personal prediction guarantee.

Time-dependent AUC requires a named horizon, event-by-time cases, event-free controls and appropriate handling of incomplete follow-up. It is not interchangeable with a differently defined survival C-index. Evaluate locked predictions against reference outcomes on independent data, retain the estimator, uncertainty, case mix and censoring method, and examine relevant subgroups. Training-only performance and changed outcome definitions can mislead. Discrimination can change with population heterogeneity; it establishes neither calibrated risks, false-call consequences nor benefit from model-guided care.

ROC-AUC and precision-recall area summarize different features. In a thought experiment that changes prevalence while holding the case and non-case score distributions fixed, sensitivity and specificity at each threshold, and thus the ROC curve, stay fixed while precision changes. Actual population shifts can change those conditional distributions too, so ROC-AUC is not universally immune to case mix. A precision-recall curve can be informative for rare positive outcomes without being a universally superior summary for every task.

Not the pharmacokinetic AUC: in pharmacology 'AUC' also names the area under a drug concentration-time curve, a measure of exposure, which is unrelated to the area under a ROC or precision-recall curve (FDA clinical pharmacology labelling guidance lists AUC among exposure measures).

records.name: C-index (concordance index), Harrell's and Uno's
records.tldr: A concordance measure checks whether predicted ordering agrees with observed outcome ordering. Survival versions must specify how follow-up and censoring are handled.
records.summary: A survival C-index assesses whether a person predicted at higher risk experiences the event earlier in informative pairs. The estimand, follow-up horizon, handling of ties, comparable pairs and censoring assumptions matter. Harrell-style observed-pair estimates can depend on the censoring distribution. Uno and colleagues proposed a censoring-adjusted concordance estimator under stated assumptions. Neither version establishes calibrated probabilities or removes every source of follow-up bias.

links.label: Harrell et al., Evaluating the yield of medical tests (JAMA 1982)
Uno et al., On the C-statistics for evaluating overall adequacy of risk prediction procedures with censored survival data (Statistics in Medicine 2011)

notes: Uno's 2011 method targets concordance within a prespecified follow-up period. Its basic derivation assumes censoring is independent of event time and predictors. It weights usable event pairs by the inverse square of the estimated probability of remaining uncensored at the earlier event time; that probability is estimated from the censoring distribution. This is not a claim that any amount or cause of missing follow-up is repaired, or that censoring always biases an unadjusted C-index upward. State the estimator, horizon and assumptions with its uncertainty.

Fictional survival scores predict earlier events at higher values. A has score 0.8 and an event at month 2; C has score 0.5 and an event at month 4, so their order is concordant. B has score 0.2 and is censored at month 1, leaving B's later event order relative to A or C unknown. B cannot be called event-free at month 4. Censoring does not automatically make a person a control, and a censored observation can still contribute to other informative comparisons when its timing permits.

records.name: Calibration: reliability diagrams and the Brier score
records.tldr: Calibration checks whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies for the same population, outcome and time horizon. Correct ranking or a correct overall average is insufficient.
records.summary: Calibration compares predicted probabilities with observed outcome frequencies in a defined population and time horizon. A model can rank people well while overstating their risks. Calibration curves and suitable summaries assess agreement with uncertainty. The Brier score averages squared differences between predicted probabilities and individual binary outcomes; it assesses overall prediction error rather than calibration alone. Incomplete follow-up and competing events need methods matched to the predicted outcome.

links.label: Wikipedia: Brier score
Graf et al., Assessment and comparison of prognostic classification schemes for survival data (Statistics in Medicine 1999)
Wikipedia
Calibration: the Achilles heel of predictive analytics.
Evaluation of clinical prediction models (part 2): how to undertake an external validation study.

notes: Compare predicted and observed frequencies across risk groups or a flexible calibration curve, with finite-sample uncertainty. Calibration-in-the-large compares the average prediction with the overall outcome rate. Under the named calibration model, slope below 1 suggests predictions that are too extreme and above 1 insufficient spread; intercept near 0 and slope near 1 still do not guarantee agreement everywhere on a flexible curve. A constant prediction can match average risk without ranking anyone. Conversely, high discrimination does not establish probability accuracy.

Two fictional 100-person groups have complete five-year outcomes. Predicting 20 and 40 per cent when 10 and 30 events occur preserves their group order but predicts 60 events instead of 40. In a second independent example, predictions of 10 and 50 per cent with 20 and 40 events give 60 predicted and 60 observed overall, or 30 per cent of 200, while both group predictions remain wrong. These invented comparisons illustrate distinct failures; they do not forecast a particular patient's outcome.

Retain predictions stored before outcomes, model and assay versions, endpoint, target population, treatment era and horizon. Compare frequencies at the same time using a calibration curve or named summary and uncertainty. Treating people censored before the horizon as event-free can mislead; account for incomplete follow-up and relevant competing events. Changed eligibility, care or baseline outcome frequency can change calibration, and an updated model needs evaluation. Checking only an overall average or displaying a narrow numerical range establishes little about model or input uncertainty. Calibration neither identifies which individual will have an event nor establishes benefit from acting on the model.

records.name: Positive predictive value (PPV)
records.tldr: Positive predictive value is the fraction of positive results that match the reference condition rather than being false positive calls. It depends on prevalence and the test's actual performance.
records.summary: Positive predictive value is the proportion of positive test calls that meet a specified reference condition: true positives divided by true plus false positives. A positive result can be a true positive or a false positive; a false positive is a positive call in someone without that reference condition. Negative predictive value uses negative calls as its denominator. These differ from sensitivity and specificity, which start with reference-condition groups. The population base rate, reference standard, threshold and actual assay performance determine how the fractions should be interpreted.

links.label: Wikipedia
FDA: statistical guidance for reporting diagnostic-test studies

notes: Separate the index-test result from a defined reference condition. Sensitivity is TP/(TP+FN), the positive fraction among reference cases; specificity is TN/(TN+FP), the negative fraction among reference non-cases. PPV is TP/(TP+FP), the reference-case fraction among positive calls; NPV is TN/(TN+FN), the reference-noncase fraction among negative calls. Base rate means prevalence of that reference condition in the intended tested population. Regrouping the same people by positive calls changes a denominator without adding participants.

Fictional groups each contain 1,000 people, with complete reference assessment, no indeterminate results and assumed sensitivity 80 per cent and specificity 90 per cent. At 10 per cent prevalence there are TP 80, FN 20, FP 90 and TN 810: PPV is 80/170, about 47.1 per cent, and NPV 810/830, about 97.6 per cent. At 50 per cent prevalence the counts are 400, 100, 50 and 450: PPV is 88.9 and NPV 81.8 per cent. At 5 per cent prevalence there are 40 true and 95 false positive calls, giving PPV 29.6 per cent. The examples hold performance fixed to isolate base rate; real populations can change performance too. High NPV can coexist with missed cases and is not a universal absence-of-disease guarantee.

Use test results and suitable independent reference outcomes in the intended population. Keep the locked threshold, condition definition, assay version, all four counts, confidence intervals and handling of missing or indeterminate results. Verifying only positive calls, using an imperfect comparator or borrowing another population's prevalence can mislead. Without a reference that establishes the condition, positive and negative percent agreement may be the appropriate descriptions; agreement does not prove either method correct. Imaging and pathological response are different assessments, so a comparison needs the population, regimen, definition, timing and surgical reference. Accuracy alone establishes neither treatment benefit nor safe surgery omission, and population fractions are not automatic personal probabilities.

records.name: Phase 1, 2 and 3 trials
records.tldr: Phase 1 studies dosage and safety; phase 3 compares treatments, often in hundreds or thousands of participants. The protocol determines the design and size, and a phase 3 label is not approval or a promise of benefit.
records.summary: Clinical-trial phases describe development purposes rather than a fixed sample size, assignment method or promise of benefit. Phase 1 studies administration, exposure, safety and dosage, sometimes with early activity measures. Phase 2 asks whether activity and safety support further study in a specified population. Phase 3 compares with a defined alternative and can provide evidence for an approval decision; a phase 3 label is not itself approval. FDA's patient overview illustrates phase 3 with hundreds to thousands of participants, while the actual size follows the protocol's question and information requirements. Phase 4 studies an approved treatment in broader use. Read the protocol because phases can overlap or be combined.

links.label: Wikipedia
FDA: clinical research phases
NCI: how clinical trials work
ICH E9: statistical principles for clinical trials, 1998
Adaptive Randomization of Neratinib in Early Breast Cancer
Adaptive Randomization of Veliparib–Carboplatin Treatment in Breast Cancer
I-SPY 2: an adaptive breast cancer trial design in the setting of neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
ClinicalTrials.gov: overall and site recruitment status fields

notes: A phase 1 activity signal neither establishes benefit nor excludes serious toxicity. A phase 2 study may be single-arm or randomized, and phase 3 may ask superiority or a prespecified non-inferiority question. Sample size follows the question and power or information assumptions; phase number alone does not determine it. A higher phase does not guarantee that a new treatment wins or that one participant benefits. Studying an approved product in phase 4 does not approve every investigated use. A single-arm study has one intervention group; identify its actual external comparison, if any, and endpoint.

I-SPY 2 illustrates an adaptively randomized phase 2 platform. Its 2016 neratinib report describes assignment within biomarker subtypes based on Bayesian probabilities of treatment superiority over control; its veliparib-carboplatin report also describes adaptive assignment within subtype. These are properties of that platform, not every phase 2 trial. Recruitment status is another distinct question: overall recruiting status does not establish an available local cohort slot or that a particular person meets the protocol.

records.name: Randomised trial
records.tldr: A study that assigns eligible participants to interventions by chance. This reduces treatment-selection bias but does not guarantee identical groups, flawless follow-up or benefit.
records.summary: A randomized trial assigns eligible consenting participants to interventions by chance. Concealing the next assignment protects enrolment against foreknowledge; blinding concerns awareness after assignment. These are different design features. Randomization reduces treatment-selection confounding but leaves possible chance imbalance, missing outcomes and limits on applicability. The comparator, endpoint, analysis and conduct determine what the comparison establishes.

links.label: Wikipedia
CONSORT statement: reporting randomised trials
CONSORT 2025 statement: Updated guideline for reporting randomised trials.
ICH E9: statistical principles for clinical trials, 1998
ICH E10: choice of control group

notes: Concealed chance assignment is different from predictable alternation between A and B. Allocation concealment hides the next assignment during enrolment; blinding concerns who knows the assigned treatment afterwards and may not be feasible for every intervention. Report sequence generation, allocation, who was blinded, assigned-group analyses, exclusions, dropout, missing assessments, treatment changes and unequal follow-up. Chance can balance measured and unmeasured factors on average without guaranteeing identical groups in one trial. Random assignment is not random sampling from a population: consenting eligible volunteers remain selected.

Controls can be standard care, standard care plus placebo or another protocol-defined option, not automatically no treatment. A fictional single-group Drug A study showing shrinkage supports an activity question for further study; it does not isolate added survival benefit from selection, natural history and other care. A randomized A-plus-usual-care versus usual-care comparison can test the added effect under sound conduct and analysis, while a volunteer cannot choose their randomized assignment or be promised benefit. A chance-assigned two-group phase 2 trial is randomized even though it is not phase 3.

records.name: Preclinical
records.tldr: Evidence from laboratory, animal and computational work used to study mechanisms, activity and safety. It can guide human studies without establishing patient benefit.
records.summary: Preclinical and nonclinical work studies mechanisms, activity, exposure and safety using specified models. Such experiments can occur before or alongside human studies. Evidence that a model responds does not establish a useful treatment for patients. FDA nonclinical requirements depend on the product and context; its published approaches include justified reductions or replacements of animal studies, so a universal two-species requirement is inaccurate.

links.label: Wikipedia
Studying cancer immunotherapy using patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) in humanized mice
What exactly is 'N' in cell culture and animal experiments?
The ARRIVE guidelines 2.0: Updated guidelines for reporting animal research.
FDA: purpose and safety context of preclinical research
FDA: context-specific nonclinical studies and new approach methodologies
Reporting animal research: Explanation and elaboration for the ARRIVE guidelines 2.0.

notes: In-vitro, in-vivo and human-derived describe experimental setting or origin, not validation of treatment in patients. A cell line can test a direct cell effect, while an immune-intact mouse can test selected tissue and immune interactions; neither reproduces every human cancer, prior treatment or physiology. An immune mechanism needs its relevant components represented and functional. Human tissue grown in a dish or grafted into a mouse remains model evidence about that intervention.

Name the intervention, control, outcome and units before counting replication. The biological unit is the entity about which conclusions are sought, such as a donor. The experimental unit receives an independently assigned intervention; the observational unit is measured. A cage assigned together or a preparation treated before being split can make the animals or wells subsamples. More measured cells do not become more assigned mice. Biological and technical replicate labels vary, so inspect sampling, preparation, allocation and measurement. Repeating runs tests consistency without adding donor identities. Analysing correlated subsamples as independent replicates is pseudoreplication.

Fictional design: each of two donors supplies six wells, three control and three treated. The twelve distinct wells receive independent randomized assignments within donor, separate treatment and no mutual influence, while the analysis retains donor nesting. There are twelve assigned wells and two donor sources, not twelve donors. No cell counts or recommended sample size are supplied. If instead a donor preparation is treated before being split, its wells are subsamples of that assignment. Adding cells does not add wells or donors. This distinction follows from the stipulated allocation, not from a universal rule that wells always are independent.

A controlled fictional mouse study in which local treatment changes a distant tumour can support a distant effect in that model. If a controlled immune-cell depletion reduces that effect, it supports a contribution under those tested conditions. Further steps include safely achievable human exposure, relevant target biology, safety and comparative patient outcomes. Mouse tumour volume is not patient survival, and a laboratory effect size or universal model threshold does not establish clinical benefit. A reproducible mechanism can coexist with an impractical or harmful clinical exposure. These are limits on the inference, not a guarantee that any particular model result will translate.

Retain the model or specimen, treatment and comparator, assigned units and subsamples, exclusions, allocation, blinded assessment, timing, dose, readout units and uncertainty. A cell count, cubic-millimetre tumour volume and named assay signal are different measurements. ARRIVE supports appraisal of animal-study reporting rather than proving a conclusion. Exploratory academic experiments and regulatory safety studies have different purposes and requirements. FDA's context-specific nonclinical approaches, including new approach methodologies, do not validate every model for personal treatment selection.

records.name: In vitro and in vivo
records.tldr: Experimental settings describe where and how a test occurs: laboratory culture, removed living material, a living organism or a computational model.
records.summary: In vitro and ex vivo describe work outside the original organism, with terminology varying by preparation and expansion. In vivo refers to work within a living organism, including animals and people; in silico refers to computation. Each setting includes different components and omits others. The label does not establish a universal ranking, human safety or treatment benefit.

links.label: Wikipedia
Source for experimental setting and intended-use interpretation
Source for experimental setting and intended-use interpretation
What exactly is 'N' in cell culture and animal experiments?
FDA: context-specific nonclinical studies and new approach methodologies

notes: Setting comparison. In vitro describes laboratory work outside the body, including grown cells and many expanded organoid assays. Ex vivo commonly describes removed living material studied outside its original organism, often briefly with retained local structure. Authors use overlapping terminology, so inspect preparation, expansion and timing. In vivo includes experiments in animals or people; identify species and host. In silico computes a prediction from data rather than directly measuring the predicted response. These terms describe where and how the experiment occurs, not a quality ranking.

Read each omitted compartment. A tumour-only dish lacks required immune interactions unless those populations are added and shown functional. A fresh slice may retain resident neighbours while losing blood flow and recruitment from circulation. A conventional PDX adds mouse circulation, exposure and metabolism without reproducing an intact human immune system. A computational prediction depends on its data, assumptions and benchmark. Human-derived tissue can be used in both dish and animal models; do not claim that ex vivo is the only setting using human tissue. A living specimen can lose cells, adapt or undergo selection after removal; retaining a structure is not retaining complete physiology. In-vitro preparations can isolate direct effects, compare doses and drugs and support repeats, while omitting perfused blood supply, host metabolism and the original population mix unless specifically reconstructed. Latin labels such as in glass, out of the living and in the living are mnemonics for setting, not quality grades.

Primary timing examples. Ladan's breast-slice assay used three-day exposures, a stated planned result window of seven to fourteen days, not a measured turnaround distribution and 23/30 usable tests from tumour-containing biopsies. Izumchenko reported 578/1,163 established PDXs and mean 16 weeks from engraftment to exposure, not biopsy to final decision. Ahlmann-Eltze compared gene-perturbation transcriptome predictions with simple baselines; the deep-learning methods did not outperform the simple linear baselines in the tested expression-prediction tasks. This was not a measured patient drug response. None of these examples shows benefit from choosing a treatment using the model. Sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10542784/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5834154/ ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40759747/

Terminology scope. NCI's ex vivo dictionary entry describes removal, treatment and return of cells or tissue to the body. That return step distinguishes cell-engineering procedures from laboratory drug testing where the tested sample is not returned. Dosing an animal and later treating removed graft cells in a dish are different experiments. Source: https://www.cancer.gov/publications/dictionaries/cancer-terms/def/ex-vivo

Regulatory scope. FDA's roadmap to reduce animal testing concerns preclinical safety development, initially focusing on monoclonal antibodies and considering human-based laboratory and computational methods. It is not approval of every organ chip or a recommendation for personal treatment selection. Source: https://www.fda.gov/files/newsroom/published/roadmap_to_reducing_animal_testing_in_preclinical_safety_studies.pdf Decision time limits which preparation is usable: establishing a new conventional PDX generally will not fit a decision due in three weeks, while a characterised short-term assay might fit but can still fail. A treatment needing liver activation also needs the relevant metabolic setting represented; a fresh slice alone omits it. Computation can rank hypotheses without growing a model, but a universal fastest or cheapest claim is not established by the setting label.

Fictional reading exercise. Compare a graft dosed in a mouse, a fresh human slice exposed outside the body and a computed sensitivity prediction. Identify actual measurement versus prediction, host, retained cells, omitted physiology and clock before drawing an inference. These settings can start from the same tumour; days, weeks or months are illustrative scales rather than guaranteed timelines. No setting is a later validation rung of another.

An experimental setting and the origin of the material are separate descriptions. Human-derived cells can be studied in vitro, briefly ex vivo or as a graft in vivo. Living-organism work includes animals and people; it does not automatically mean a human clinical trial. Preclinical intervention experiments can continue alongside human studies, so the date relative to a first human dose alone does not validate their treatment claim.

records.name: N-of-1 trial
records.tldr: A planned comparison within one person, often using repeated treatment periods. Lasting effects and changes over time can make the comparison uninterpretable.
records.summary: An N-of-1 trial studies an individual under a planned comparison. In the multiple-crossover form, treatment periods are assigned within one person and the same outcome is measured repeatedly. Suitability depends on the condition, treatment reversibility, timing and analysis. A sequence of care followed by improvement is not automatically such a trial, and a result for one person does not establish an average effect in a wider population.

links.label: Wikipedia
Wikipedia
Araujo, Julious and Senn: variation and analysis in N-of-1 trials (2016)
Liao and colleagues: N-of-1 carryover and correlated measurements (2021 preprint, version 1)

notes: Specify the question, treatments, period lengths, assigned order, background care, units, observation times and analysis before interpreting results. Inspect whether the actual design uses crossover, random order and blinding. Within-person comparison can reduce between-person differences, but it needs a sufficiently stable condition and interpretable onset and ending of effects. Carryover means an earlier treatment affects a later period; a period effect is change over time apart from the compared treatment, and nearby measurements can be correlated. Random order does not erase these problems. Choose timing and analysis for the actual design and missing observations; there is no universal washout duration.

Fictional symptom example: a planned randomized sequence A, B, B, A uses repeated measurements of the same symptom. The sequence alone proves neither benefit nor adequate transitions between periods. If A persists into B, an apparent A-versus-B contrast may mix current and earlier effects. Progression, lasting immune effects or an irreversible procedure can prevent a meaningful crossover. A cancer-treatment history with surgery and continuing therapy cannot simply be reversed into an untreated comparison. These are interpretation examples, not instructions to change or interrupt care; clinical and research oversight remain separate.

records.name: Pre-specified vs post-hoc analysis
records.tldr: An analysis planned before access to the relevant results differs from one developed afterwards. Either can be informative, but its evidence role, timing and search must be clear.
records.summary: Prespecification records an analysis question and method before access to the relevant results. Protocols, statistical analysis plans and dated amendments distinguish confirmatory questions from planned exploration and later discoveries. A prespecified analysis can still be exploratory or imprecise. A post-hoc analysis can generate useful hypotheses, but choosing a favourable result and then calling it prespecified or independently validated does not provide confirmation.

links.label: Wikipedia
CONSORT 2025 statement: Updated guideline for reporting randomised trials.
ICH E9: statistical principles for clinical trials, 1998
The ASA Statement on p-Values: Context, Process, and Purpose

notes: Keep the dated protocol and analysis plan, endpoint and starting clock, population, methods, marker rule, evidence role and multiplicity strategy. Record amendments, their reasons and access to unblinded results. An amendment made without relevant outcome access differs from choosing an analysis after seeing a favourable result. Planning cannot supply missing events or precision, and a prespecified exploratory question remains exploratory. A plan uploaded after results calls for earlier versions and access dates; that timing alone establishes neither misconduct nor confirmation.

Fictional analysis example: event-free survival is the primary endpoint, a marker subgroup is planned as exploratory, and after opening the results investigators search 12 additional cutoffs and select the smallest p-value. Keep all three evidence roles and the entire 12-cutoff search. The schematic choices contain no supplied p-values or measured threshold coordinates. Locking the discovered cutoff permits an appropriate independent test; it neither changes the original analysis role nor confirms treatment-selection utility by itself.

A p-value describes compatibility of the data with a specified statistical model under its assumptions. It is not the probability that the subgroup claim is true. Selection among many analyses changes how an attractive p-value should be interpreted.

records.name: Subgroup analysis (forest plots)
records.tldr: A subgroup analysis compares effects in defined groups. A striking estimate or different significance labels do not by themselves establish that treatment effects differ.
records.summary: Subgroup analyses examine whether treatment effects differ across defined groups. Report the effect scale, interaction analysis, uncertainty, multiplicity and whether the groups and methods were specified before relevant results were available. Wide intervals, selected cutoffs and missing specimens can limit interpretation. A significant result in one group and a nonsignificant result in another is not itself a test of their difference. Confirmation and treatment-selection utility require additional evidence.

links.label: Wikipedia
Biomarker: Predictive or Prognostic?
CONSORT 2025 statement: Updated guideline for reporting randomised trials.
ICH E9: statistical principles for clinical trials, 1998

notes: A small subgroup chosen because of its observed result can motivate a new study without establishing who benefits from treatment. Compare treatment-effect estimates directly using an appropriate interaction analysis, uncertainty and multiplicity control; different significance labels in two groups are not evidence that the effects differ. A group defined by response after treatment is also different from a baseline category because treatment can affect who enters it.

records.name: Group sequential design, stopping rules and alpha spending
records.tldr: A trial design that plans comparisons before completion and controls overall false-positive error. Each look has rules for interpreting its accumulated information.
records.summary: Group sequential designs plan comparisons before a trial is complete while controlling the overall false-positive probability. The schedule, information fraction and stopping rules belong to that trial and endpoint. Benefit, safety and futility monitoring can use different criteria, and an early p-value need not be judged against 0.05. Independent monitoring and confidentiality help protect conduct while results accumulate.

links.label: Wikipedia
Wikipedia

FDA guidance: adaptive designs for clinical trials of drugs and biologics
ICH E9: statistical principles for clinical trials, 1998
Pembrolizumab for Early Triple-Negative Breast Cancer.

notes: ICH E9 defines an interim analysis as a pre-completion comparison of treatment arms for efficacy or safety and recommends planning it in advance. An unplanned comparison still is an interim analysis; E9 calls for justification and assessment of its bias, with an amendment before unblinded access when a new analysis is introduced. Record the endpoint, schedule, stopping rules, information fraction and its basis. Event-driven information uses accumulated versus planned events, not median follow-up alone. Overall error control, often through alpha spending, accounts for repeated looks. Safety, efficacy and futility rules serve different purposes. Preserve the actual monitoring and confidentiality procedures rather than assuming that every study uses the same committee or boundary.

Historical trial examples show why the endpoint and look matter. KEYNOTE-522 first assessed pathological complete response among the first 602 randomized participants; its fourth planned interim event-free-survival analysis had median follow-up of 39.1 months. OlympiA initially reported 59 versus 86 deaths, hazard ratio 0.68 and P = 0.02, which did not cross its P < 0.01 interim boundary. Its second overall-survival analysis used P < 0.015 and reported P = 0.009. CREATE-X met its primary endpoint at a prespecified interim analysis and stopped early. These endpoints and looks have their own maturity and rules; not crossing an early boundary does not establish no effect.

Bassler and colleagues compared 91 trials stopped early for benefit, covering 63 questions, with 424 matched trials not stopped early. The pooled ratio of relative risks was 0.71, with 95 per cent confidence interval 0.65 to 0.77, indicating larger apparent effects in the early-stopped trials. The difference was independent of whether a stopping rule was used and greatest in smaller studies; large differences occurred with fewer than 500 events. This meta-epidemiological result is not a correction factor to apply to every trial.

Fictional two-look example: P = 0.03 does not cross a first-look efficacy boundary of P < 0.01. Benefit has not been established at that look. It does not follow that there is no treatment effect or that a later look has the same threshold.

records.name: Futility analysis (stopped for futility)
records.tldr: A monitoring judgment that the trial is unlikely to meet its planned success criterion. It does not prove that the treatments are equal.
records.summary: Futility monitoring asks whether continuing a trial is unlikely to demonstrate its prespecified success criterion with the remaining information. The criterion can concern superiority or non-inferiority; the method and boundary belong to the protocol, not a universal conditional-power percentage. A monitoring committee can recommend stopping, but its actual rule and decision matter. A futility stop, a safety stop and a sponsor decision for poor accrual or business reasons are different explanations.

links.label: Wikipedia

Randomized Phase III Postoperative Trial of Platinum-Based Chemotherapy Versus Capecitabine in Patients With Residual Triple-Negative Breast Cancer Following Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy: ECOG-ACRIN EA1131.

notes: EA1131 compared adjuvant platinum with capecitabine after neoadjuvant therapy for residual triple-negative breast cancer, using a non-inferiority design with a superiority alternative for the basal subtype. At 120 invasive disease-free-survival events, 61 per cent of planned information, the monitoring committee judged further follow-up unlikely to establish platinum non-inferiority or superiority. Three-year invasive disease-free survival was 42 per cent with platinum and 49 per cent with capecitabine. This stop concerns that planned success criterion; it does not establish equal arms or the absence of every real difference.

records.name: Real-world evidence
records.tldr: Evidence about use, benefit or risk derived from analysis of routinely collected health data. Treatment assignment and comparison design determine what it can establish.
records.summary: Real-world data are routinely collected information about health and care; real-world evidence is clinical evidence about a product's use, benefits or risks derived from analysing such data. Records, claims and registries can describe care beyond tightly selected trials. An observational comparison does not assign treatment, so its causal interpretation depends on how groups, outcomes and follow-up are constructed, measured and analysed. More data can improve precision while leaving systematic bias.

links.label: Wikipedia
FDA real-world evidence programme
The Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) statement: guidelines for reporting observational studies.
Specifying a target trial prevents immortal time bias and other self-inflicted injuries in observational analyses
Empirical confidence interval calibration for population-level effect estimation studies in observational healthcare data

notes: An observational study records or reconstructs exposures without assigning them. A cohort follows a defined group over time; a case-control design selects people with and without an outcome and examines earlier exposures; a cross-sectional design measures a population at a time point. Prospective means forward follow-up, not randomized assignment. Such data can describe uncommon harms, care patterns and underrepresented populations. A causal claim about changing treatment requires more than an association. Random assignment reduces treatment-selection bias but cannot guarantee complete follow-up or applicability. In a fictional database, following treated and untreated groups forward from different dates does not randomize them.

When emulating a trial, align eligibility, treatment-strategy assignment and the start of follow-up. Requiring treated people to survive until treatment while starting comparison follow-up earlier can build in a survival advantage. Matching, restriction and statistical adjustment require suitable measurements, assumptions and overlap; poorly measured or unmeasured factors can remain. A large database does not remove systematic error from confounding, selection or measurement. Inspect missing outcomes and follow-up as well as the starting clock.

Two reading rules follow from asking which comparison is being estimated. A consequence of treatment is not automatically a baseline cause of treatment selection, so adjusting for every recorded variable is not a universal remedy and can change the question. Also check the proposed direction of time and causation: developing disease might change an exposure rather than the exposure initiating the disease. These are alternative explanations to examine in a particular study, not findings that either occurred in every observational dataset.

records.name: Publication format and peer-review status
records.tldr: Whether a claim comes from a conference abstract, a preprint or a full journal article tells you how much of the study you can inspect and what review it has had, but not whether the study is valid.
records.summary: Publication format and review status describe what can be inspected and what scrutiny a report has received. A conference abstract, preprint, full article and correction can report different versions of one study. Identify the study and version, read the available methods and match every result to its population, endpoint and data cutoff. Peer review adds scrutiny; it does not establish that every conclusion is correct or independently replicated.

links.label: ICMJE: corrections and version control
CONSORT for reporting randomised trials in journal and conference abstracts: explanation and elaboration (PLOS Medicine 2008)
CONSORT 2025: updated guideline for reporting randomised trials (PLOS Medicine)

notes: A conference abstract or presentation can offer early findings with limited methods; inspect any poster or slides separately. A preprint is a versioned manuscript released before completed journal peer review. A full article usually permits more inspection, including its supplement, protocol and analysis plan, but can still have missing information or exploratory analyses. An abstract may also be the summary of a full article, so its existence does not make evidence conference-only. Editorial peer review, conference selection and independent replication are different forms of scrutiny, and newer does not automatically mean better designed. A study report, news release and commentary are different source types.

Keep the study identifier, document type, date and version, recruited population, denominator, endpoint and starting clock, data cutoff and follow-up, analysis role and location of methods. Check corrections and retractions at the publisher and inspect the affected claim. ICMJE recommends a correction notice detailing changes, a dated updated version and an archive of prior versions. A full paper with an abstract and later correction should be identified as that sequence, not called conference-only. This checking sequence makes limitations visible; it does not certify validity.

Fictional publication example: an early report describes 12 responses among 20 participants, while a later full report includes 30 participants and longer follow-up. Both can be accurate for their cutoffs. Do not combine the early response percentage with the later follow-up as one estimate, or treat overlapping participants as independent confirmation. New methods or comparator details can change interpretation, but publishing a single-group study in full does not create a randomized control group.

records.name: Case report
records.tldr: A case report describes what happened to one person or a few, which can reveal a signal or a harm but cannot show what would have happened under a different treatment.
records.summary: A case report documents a clinical course, interventions, outcomes and alternative explanations. It can reveal a signal of benefit or harm without establishing what would have happened under another approach. The CARE reporting guideline includes a timeline, diagnostic assessment, interventions, follow-up, the patient perspective and consent; complete reporting supports appraisal rather than proving treatment causation.

links.label: CARE guidelines: consensus-based clinical case reporting guideline (Deutsches Arzteblatt 2013)
CENT 2015: CONSORT extension for reporting N-of-1 trials (BMJ)

notes: A careful case timeline can preserve an unusual experience and generate questions. Published memorable successes do not supply all treated people as a denominator, so they cannot establish a response probability or treatment ranking. Several scans in one person remain observations from one person. A report usually lacks the concurrent counterfactual outcome under another treatment, and even a rigorous individual comparison would not establish the average effect in everyone sharing a cancer label.

Fictional clinical history: treatment A starts, a procedure is added, treatment B starts and a later scan improves. This establishes improvement during that course, not the separate added contributions of the procedure or B. The earlier treatment, procedure and later treatment can have overlapping lasting influences. Drawing overlapping ribbons represents that possibility and ordering only; it supplies no measured effect size or known duration. Documenting experience and planning an interpretable comparison are different routes to evidence.

records.name: Meta-analysis
records.tldr: A meta-analysis combines estimates from separate studies with a stated statistical method; it can improve precision, but it cannot repair studies that answer different questions or share the same biases.
records.summary: A meta-analysis statistically combines estimates from studies addressing a sufficiently compatible question. It can be part of a systematic review, which explicitly finds, selects and appraises studies; pooling is not compulsory. The result depends on the studies, their biases, effect definitions, model and weights. A precise pooled mean need not describe every setting or an individual person.

links.label: Higgins, Thompson and Spiegelhalter: a re-evaluation of random-effects meta-analysis (JRSS A 2009)
Cochrane Handbook chapter 10: analysing data and undertaking meta-analyses
PRISMA 2020 statement: reporting systematic reviews (BMJ 2021)
Specifying a target trial prevents immortal time bias and other self-inflicted injuries in observational analyses

notes: A common-effect model targets one underlying effect, while a random-effects model describes a distribution of study effects and its mean. Weights follow the stated estimator, not simply the largest participant count. Clinical and methodological differences, bias and heterogeneity beyond sampling error need investigation; a random-effects calculation does not remove them or make incompatible studies comparable.

A confidence interval for the mean effect differs from a prediction interval for an underlying effect in another comparable study under the model. Neither is a personal prognosis interval. I-squared estimates the proportion of variability in study estimates associated with heterogeneity rather than sampling error; it is neither the percentage of people helped nor the percentage of studies that are wrong. Tau-squared is between-study effect variance on the chosen scale, such as squared score points or squared log risk ratios. These estimates can be uncertain, especially with few studies, and no I-squared cutoff alone makes pooling safe.

Fictional forest example: five studies compare treatment A minus control on the same 0 to 100 symptom scale at day 30. Their effects are -8, -6, -4, -2 and 0 points, each with standard error 2 and weight 20 per cent, so the square areas are equal. The mean is -4.0 points. With a classical moment variance estimate, Q = 10, I-squared = 60 per cent and tau-squared = 6 squared score points. A normal 95 per cent mean interval is about -6.8 to -1.2; the stated 2009 prediction method, using a t distribution with three degrees of freedom, gives about -13.0 to +5.0. The study intervals, mean diamond and wider prediction interval answer different questions. Five studies are few and these intervals are approximate; a negative mean does not imply a negative effect in every setting.

Retain search dates, eligibility, unique study identities, risk of bias, treatment sequence, event definition, starting clock, horizon, effect scale, model, weights, uncertainty and sensitivity analyses. Abstracts, full reports and follow-up of the same participants are linked reports rather than independently weighted trials. Availability related to findings can leave evidence missing. Pooling observational associations does not create randomization or establish one person's treatment benefit. PRISMA promotes transparent reporting; completing its checklist does not certify validity.

Fictional weighted example: two comparable three-year risk differences are -4 and -8 percentage points with supplied weights 0.75 and 0.25. Their weighted mean is -5 points; these stipulated weights are not claimed precision estimates. Correct arithmetic would still not justify pooling if one study starts at randomization and another selects responders at a later landmark. The eligibility, clock and target question must be compared first.

records.name: Controlled perturbation experiment
records.tldr: A controlled perturbation changes one defined factor in an experiment and compares the response with control conditions, so that the change can be told apart from background, carrier effects and assay failure.
records.summary: A controlled perturbation deliberately changes a defined factor and measures the response against appropriate comparison conditions. Vehicle, positive, negative and mechanism controls answer different questions. A reproducible response can support an experimental claim without establishing its proposed mechanism or patient benefit. Baseline growth, timing, dose and the actual unit assigned to treatment matter.

links.label: Hafner et al.: growth rate inhibition metrics correct for confounders in measuring drug sensitivity (Nature Methods 2016)
Measuring cancer drug sensitivity and resistance in cultured cells (Current Protocols in Chemical Biology 2017)
The promise and peril of chemical probes
What exactly is 'N' in cell culture and animal experiments?

notes: A vehicle control contains the carrier without the active treatment; an untreated condition asks a different question if the carrier has effects. A positive control checks that the assay can detect a known relevant response, while a negative or non-targeting control estimates background under its design. Another independent way to disrupt the same function can support a mechanism, and a rescue restores a function to test whether that reverses the response here. Off-target effects, incomplete restoration and model context limit interpretation. These are questions for matched model, timing and readout; no one control proves specificity or patient benefit, and agreement between similar readouts is not automatically independent mechanistic confirmation.

Keep what changed, the comparator, concentration or dose range, timing, assignment, readout and units, sample identities, replicate structure and variability. Repeated wells address variation under their preparation and allocation; independently obtained biological samples address another source of variation. Many wells from one tumour do not become independent patients, and repetition or a small p-value does not repair a missing comparison. A two-drug experiment needs vehicle, both single drugs and the combination. A larger combination effect than either single drug is not automatically synergy; that claim needs a stated reference model.

Fictional direct counts: vehicle-treated cells increase from 100 to 200 while drug-treated cells remain at 100. The endpoint drug count is half the vehicle count without measured net decline from the starting count, so calling it 50 per cent killing overstates the observation. Slower growth, death and a molecular change require their own readouts; direct death or recovery measurements could address further questions. Hafner and colleagues showed that conventional IC50 and maximal-effect measures depend on cell divisions during an assay and developed growth-rate metrics to address that dependence. A real experimental response does not by itself establish the responsible target or clinical benefit.

records.name: False discovery rate
records.tldr: The false discovery rate is the expected fraction of false findings among the findings a procedure selects, counted as zero when nothing is selected; it describes the shortlist as a set, not any one result.
records.summary: False discovery rate is the expected proportion of false rejections among all rejections made by a multiple-testing procedure, taking the proportion as zero when none are made. It describes repeated use of that procedure under its assumptions. It is not the probability that each selected finding is false, a guaranteed false fraction in one list or evidence of biological importance or patient benefit.

links.label: Benjamini and Hochberg: controlling the false discovery rate (Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B 1995)
Benjamini and Yekutieli: false discovery rate control under dependency (Annals of Statistics 2001)

notes: Write V for false rejections and R for all rejections: the false discovery proportion is V/R, defined as zero when R is zero, and FDR is its expectation. Family-wise error is the probability of at least one false rejection; the two coincide when every null hypothesis is true but generally differ otherwise. Benjamini-Hochberg sorts all m valid p-values, compares rank i with (i/m)q, finds the largest passing rank and selects everything through it. The original control result assumes independence; positive-dependence extensions and procedures for broader dependence have their own conditions. Correlation is not permission to ignore the procedure's assumptions.

Fictional Benjamini-Hochberg examples use target q = 0.05. For five sorted p-values 0.001, 0.008, 0.026, 0.080 and 0.200, rank bounds are 0.01, 0.02, 0.03, 0.04 and 0.05; rank 3 is the largest passing rank, selecting the first three. For three values 0.018, 0.030 and 0.060, bounds are about 0.0167, 0.0333 and 0.05; rank 1 fails its individual comparison but rank 2 passes, so the first two are selected. Do not stop at the first failure. The two illustrative plots use different labelled vertical ranges and test counts. Selection assigns neither finding a five per cent false probability.

Keep the complete hypothesis family and valid p-values, target, procedure and dependence assumptions, then report the selected set or adjusted values under that method. Correcting separate families and combining their hits does not automatically control the combined list. Q-values and adjusted p-values can name different calculations, so identify the actual method. Gene-, peptide- and protein-level identification claims also have different units; control at one level does not automatically transfer to another. The fraction of diagnostic positive calls that are false, one minus PPV, is a different quantity from the expected false-rejection fraction of a multiple-testing procedure. Omics selection prioritizes further investigation; it does not identify which hit is false or establish clinical utility.
